draft.title: Population and sample
card: the whole group being studied. It can be people, animals or things, such as all the students in a school.
a part of the population that is actually asked or measured. Its results are used to learn about the whole group.
A sample is used when asking everyone would cost too much or take too long. It may also be used when testing destroys the item.
Example: a school has 800 students. A teacher asks 40 of them about lunch. The population is all 800 students. The sample is the 40 students asked.
draft.remember: The population is everyone in the group. The sample is the part you actually ask.

a.q: A council wants to know how Year 8 students in its area get to school. It asks 150 of the 2000 Year 8 students. What is the sample?
opts: The 150 students who were asked
The 2000 Year 8 students in the area
The way each student gets to school
The council that ran the survey
a.why: The sample is the part of the group that was actually asked, which is the 150 students. The 2000 students are the whole group, so they are the population.

b.q: A battery company wants to know how long its batteries last. It tests 50 batteries from a day's output of 10,000. Why does it use a sample?
opts: Testing every battery would use them all up
The 10,000 batteries are the sample, so no more are needed
Fifty batteries are the whole population being studied
A sample always gives the same result as the population
b.why: Testing a battery until it goes flat uses it up, so testing all 10,000 would leave nothing to sell. The 50 batteries are the sample, and the 10,000 are the population. A sample may not give exactly the same result as the whole group.
b.clue: Think about what happens to a battery once it has been tested.

b.best: Testing every battery would use them all up

problems.detail: The remember line calls the population 'everyone in the group' and the sample 'the part you actually ask'. Question b is about batteries that are tested, not asked, so the remember line is narrower than the card. Suggest: 'The population is the whole group. The sample is the part you actually ask or measure.'
